There are no cascading platinum curls, no heavy false eyelashes, and no painted-on beauty marks. 

Instead, the images reveal a girl glowing in the California sun.

In one striking frame, she sits on a hillside beneath the dappled shade of a eucalyptus tree, wearing a simple, unpressed button-down shirt with the sleeves rolled to her elbows and high-waisted denim jeans. Her hair, a soft, natural honey-blonde, is tossed casually by the breeze. Her face is remarkably bare, saving for a touch of light balm on her lips. "When you look at these Griffith Park photographs, you aren't looking at 'Marilyn Monroe' the icon; you are looking at Norma Jeane in the middle of a metamorphosis," says visual historian and curator Elena Vance, who was among the first to examine the find. "There is a total absence of artifice. She is unguarded, innocent, and startlingly human."

The softness of the 1950 portraits stands in stark, poignant contrast to the image the world would come to demand of her just a few years later. 

By the mid-1950s, following breakout roles in *Gentlemen Prefer Blondes* and *The Seven Year Itch*, the studio system had fully forged the archetype of the ultimate Hollywood sex symbol. The innocent park-goer was replaced by a technicolor siren—a creature of painted-on blood-red lipstick, contoured cheekbones, skin-tight silk, and a carefully practiced, bedroom-eyed gaze. 

Where the Griffith Park photos project an easy warmth and approachable vulnerability, her later publicity stills project a dazzling, almost blinding hyper-sexuality. The world fell in love with a fantasy: the voluptuous, breathy blonde who seemed to exist purely for the male gaze. Yet, as historians have long noted, that very persona became a golden cage that swallowed the quiet, well-read young woman who once wandered through the hills of Los Angeles with bare feet and a camera crew of one.

The photographer behind the 1950 shoot was a freelance photojournalist whose archive was liquidated after his death in the late 1980s, leaving the negatives buried in storage until a routine inventory of the warehouse brought them to light last month.

She had no stylist, no entourage, and no idea that within three years she would be the most famous woman on the planet.

"There is a quiet tragedy in contrasting these early images with her later work," Vance adds. "In 1950, she was looking forward to a career, full of hope, unaffected by the suffocating weight of global obsession. In Griffith Park, she was just a young woman enjoying an afternoon in the park."

**Never-before-seen photos of a young Marilyn Monroe uncovered in LIFE archive**

By **CNN Staff**
Updated 4:15 PM EDT, August 13, 2009

**(CNN) —** Long before she was the blonde bombshell who captivated millions, Marilyn Monroe was just a 24-year-old starlet trying to make it in Hollywood — relaxed, radiant, and virtually unknown. 

Now, nearly 50 years after her tragic death, a remarkable set of lost photographs showing Monroe on the precipice of global fame has been brought to light for the very first time.

The black-and-white images, taken in 1950 by veteran *LIFE* magazine photographer Ed Clark, were recently discovered in the magazine’s vast, newly digitized archives. Published this week on Life.com, the photos offer an intimate, candid look at a young woman who had no idea she was about to become one of the most famous icons of the 20th century.

### 'Who the hell is Marilyn Monroe?'

The story behind the photos is a classic Hollywood artifact. In 1950, 20th Century Fox hired Clark to shoot a rising young actress who was generating quiet buzz in the film industry following small, standout roles in *The Asphalt Jungle* and *All About Eve*. 

Clark took Monroe to Los Angeles’ Griffith Park for a casual, outdoor photoshoot. The resulting images capture her lounging on a blanket in the grass, reading scripts, and gazing playfully into the camera. Dressed in simple, dark trousers and a button-down shirt, she appears stripped of the heavy glamour and hyper-sexualized persona that would later define her career.

"I sent the rolls into *LIFE* in New York," Clark recalled before his death in 2000. "They wired back, 'Who the hell is Marilyn Monroe?'"

At the time, the magazine’s editors decided she wasn’t famous enough to warrant a feature story. The negatives were filed away in an envelope, stashed in the *LIFE* archives, and effectively forgotten for 59 years.

### A rare look at an unmanufactured star

What makes the discovery so compelling to film historians and pop culture fans alike is the sheer naturalism of the shots. In 1950, Monroe was Norma Jeane Mortenson transitioning into "Marilyn" — she had not yet perfected the iconic breathy voice, the platinum blonde curls, or the seductive pout.

In Clark’s photos, she laughs naturally, squinting into the Southern California sun. 

"You see a vulnerability and a freshness here that was completely lost once the Hollywood studio system took hold of her," said film historian and pop-culture analyst Sarah Morrison. "In these photos, she isn't playing 'Marilyn Monroe.' She's just a young woman sitting in a park on a sunny afternoon. It’s haunting when you consider what came later."

### Digitizing history

The discovery comes as part of a massive joint project between *LIFE* and Google to digitize millions of the magazine's historic, unpublished photographs. For decades, *LIFE* boasted one of the greatest photo archives in the world, containing millions of images that never made it into print due to space constraints or editorial whims.

For photo archivists sifting through dusty drawers and negative sleeves, finding an entire unused roll of a future icon is the ultimate prize.

According to *LIFE* editors, the 1950 images show a performer who was already intimately comfortable with the camera lens. Even without the full backing of a major publicity engine, her magnetism was undeniable.

Just three years after Clark’s photos were stashed in a cabinet, Monroe would land the cover of *LIFE* magazine in 1953, cementing her status as a global superstar. By then, the girl in Griffith Park was gone, replaced by the grandest screen siren in the world.

The full gallery of the rediscovered 1950 Ed Clark photos is available to view at Life.com.
